title: Not just Proton: Getting to know Valve's new SteamOS compatibility layers
gist: Beyond Proton, Valve is shipping two new SteamOS compatibility layers for the Steam Frame headset: FEX, a Valve-funded x86-on-Arm binary recompiler, and Lepton, a Waydroid-derived container that runs Android APKs. 52 of the first 120 'Great on Frame' games run as Lepton-translated Android executables, and Valve says FEX's maturity now opens the door to SteamOS on general Arm devices.

insights.claim: FEX is Valve's port of fex-emu, an open source project that emulates x86 processor instructions on Arm chipsets, described by its own site as 'an advanced binary recompiler that supports all modern extensions of the x86(-64) instruction set.'
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Full x86-64 extension coverage on Arm is the technical precondition for moving an entire PC game catalog off Intel/AMD silicon.
insights.quote: an advanced binary recompiler that supports all modern extensions of the x86(-64) instruction set

insights.claim: The FEX emulator can make calls directly to graphics libraries like OpenGL and Vulkan to reduce overhead and uses code caching to minimize stuttering, according to Steam's own developer documentation.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Native graphics-library passthrough is the difference between a demo emulator and one usable for shipping games.
insights.quote: code caching to minimize stuttering as much as possible
insights.locator: according to Steam’s own developer documentation

insights.claim: Valve has been funding FEX lead developer Ryan Houdek since the project was a prototype in 2018, having anticipated from the outset that 'close to a decade of work' would be needed before fex-emu was robust enough to rely on.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: An eight-year funded runway before productization is a rare example of platform-level patient capital in consumer tech.
insights.quote: close to a decade of work [would be] needed before [Fex-emu] would be robust enough people could rely on it for their libraries
insights.locator: Valve engineer Pierre-Loup Griffais told The Verge last year

insights.claim: Houdek publicly credited Valve for backing the project from the start and for insisting it remain an open project anyone can adapt, rather than a Valve-only tool.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Keeping the layer open means rivals can also use it — Valve is betting on ecosystem gravity over exclusivity.
insights.quote: They trusted me with the responsibility of designing and frameworking the project in a way that it can work long-term
insights.locator: Houdek wrote last November while marking the seventh anniversary

insights.claim: With FEX now ready for integration into the Steam Frame headset, Valve says it is actively exploring versions of SteamOS for other Arm devices, with engineer Pierre-Loup Griffais describing the Frame as 'paving the way' for 'more general SteamOS for Arm.'
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: SteamOS on generic Arm hardware would widen Valve's platform beyond its own devices — watch for third-party Arm handhelds shipping SteamOS.
insights.quote: just more general SteamOS for Arm, right?
insights.locator: Griffais recently told Rock Paper Shotgun

insights.claim: Griffais frames the goal as removing the catalog-compatibility penalty from Arm hardware, so buyers never have to conclude that a device with good specs and value would force them to 'leave a portion of my catalog behind.'
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Library portability is the real moat in PC gaming; whoever solves it for Arm captures the next hardware cycle.
insights.quote: I have to leave a portion of my catalog behind if I’m even considering it
insights.locator: For Griffais, the goal is for gamers to be able to consider Arm-based hardware

insights.claim: Griffais characterizes Arm devices as an 'adjacent ecosystem that's just a little bit different. But not really that different,' signaling Valve sees low technical distance between its current platform and Arm hardware.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Valve's own framing implies a short path to expansion, not a multi-year rewrite.
insights.locator: There’s a bunch of devices where you could have a great experience running SteamOS

insights.claim: Lepton is Valve's second new compatibility layer, an expansion of the pre-existing Waydroid project that runs standard Android APKs on SteamOS inside a software container.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: An Android runtime inside SteamOS quietly makes Steam a potential distribution channel for mobile-built software.
insights.locator: The second new compatibility layer hitting Steam is Lepton

insights.claim: Lepton is necessary for the Steam Frame because many standalone VR titles players will run on the device were originally designed for the Android-based Quest headsets.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Valve is directly harvesting Meta's Quest developer ecosystem rather than asking for new ports.
insights.locator: This layer is especially necessary for the Steam Frame

insights.claim: VR.org found by digging through Steam metadata that 52 of the first 120 'Great on Frame' games run on the Steam Frame as Android executables translated via Lepton, including the first three Steam games listed without any Windows, Mac or Linux builds.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Roughly 43 percent of flagship Frame titles are Android-native — a concrete measure of how far Steam has drifted from Windows binaries.
insights.locator: VR.org dug through Steam metadata this month

insights.claim: Valve engineer Jeremy Selan said VR developers already familiar with making mobile VR APKs 'are now free to bring those to Steam, and they'll just work on this device,' removing porting cost as a barrier to publishing.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Zero-port publishing sharply lowers the content-acquisition cost for a new VR platform.
insights.quote: They are now free to bring those to Steam, and they’ll just work on this device
insights.locator: Valve engineer Jeremy Selan told The Verge last year

insights.claim: Asked whether generic Android apps and non-VR games could be shipped through Lepton, Valve's Lawrence Yang said 'We've never disinvited people from doing that' while immediately adding 'We are a games company and we are focused on games.'
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: A deliberately non-committal answer leaves open a Steam-as-Android-app-store scenario Valve is not yet endorsing.
insights.quote: We’ve never disinvited people from doing that
insights.locator: Valve’s Lawrence Yang told The Verge

insights.claim: Valve's compatibility strategy has shifted fundamentally: where the first version of SteamOS asked developers to create bespoke Linux ports, the platform now absorbs Windows, x86 and Android binaries through layered translation.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Translation layers instead of developer mandates is the repeatable playbook for a platform without market power over developers.
insights.locator: we’ve definitely come a long way since Valve was asking developers to create their own bespoke Linux ports

insights.claim: Proton, unlike FEX, was built on the pre-existing Wine conversion tool, meaning Valve's compatibility stack is assembled from three separately originated open source projects rather than built in-house from scratch.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Valve's advantage is funding and integrating open source rather than owning it — a capital-efficient platform model.
insights.locator: While Proton was based on the pre-existing Wine conversion tool
